questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I was looking for a good university with interesting modules and a different culture. I was also planning my exchange with another law student and we prioritised Belfast as it was not one of the most popular destinations. This was so that we both would have a higher chance of getting a spot at the same university. We also prioritised an english speaking country as we wanted to be as independent as possible when exploring the country. We were also looking for improving our english skills. The other law student and I got a spot at Queen's University Belfast and we travelled together.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It was a really fun exchange experience and I loved it. There is a lot of history in Belfast as the Northern Irish "capital" and the divide between Ireland and UK is very interesting. It is a smaller city and you therefore get to know the city rather quickly. People are so nice and the accent is not that hard to understand. The whole exchange process was easy and manageable, you only had to make sure to fill out all the paperwork in time. I was very happy that I chose Belfast, because it was such an interesting city that I probably would not have travelled to otherwise.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Very easy. I would receive emails from the university's exchange office and they answered any questions I had quickly. Other than that their website was good, however, it was a little bit difficult to find the page with the modules.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: They had a welcome zoom meeting with a lot of information about visas and airport transport a little before we all had to start, so if we had questions we would get the answers before travelling. When arriving, there was first a welcome week for the international students and the next week it was the welcome week for the UK students. In the welcome week we were invited to tea parties with our faculties and induction meetings with a Law professor responsible for the international students. From there we knew who to email regarding questions about our modules and assignments and so on.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: There was a little miscommunication with the arriving date regarding airport transport. We were informed that the earliest day to arrive to accommodation was the 13th of September, however, the University only provided airport transport for a few days before the 13th and after the 13th, but not on the 13th. At this point a lot of the international students (including us) had already bought our tickets on the 13th. This was not a big issue at all and we just called a taxi when arriving at the airport. The students who had not already bought their tickets, just bought them to match with a day with airport transport.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer:
Queen's University Belfast guarantee accommodation for all first year students, including international and erasmus students. You pick three out of five places you would like to live, and thereafter you get an offer. 
Queens Accommodation have several accommodations including BT9 (Elms village, which is a little outside of city centre) and BT1 and BT2 (which are in the city centre). But BT9 is closer to the University, while there is a longer walk from BT1 and BT 2. We lived in BT9 in the Oak 2 building.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: In our accommodation we shared a communal kitchen on a hall with 10 people in total. There is weekly cleaning and enough room for everyone to have room for their stuff in the kitchen. The room where the kitchen was also included a living room with a sitting area, a sofa and a TV.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer: I would definitely recommend all future exchange students to live at Queens Accommodation. Even though you share kitchen, shower and toilets with your hallway in most of BT9's accommodation, it was a great place to make new friends (its like a small town full of students). You should know that that the walls are very thin and it is therefore not really possible to have house parties, which I think only was a big thing this time because of COVID-19 and the clubs being closed throughout most of the semester. Once they opened we all went out to party.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The Queens Accommodation offer a kitchen and a bedding pack to about 35 pound each. I would not recommend buying the kitchen pack! It is not worth it at all, and you should just buy the stuff you need at tesco or Poundland. The bedding pack is not worth it either and you can find the stuff at Ikea, but I heard the trip is a bit long (i bought the bedding pack and did not go the Ikea, so don't know it its too complicated). Elms village has 24-hours-reception and you can always get help if you lock yourself out, which will happen if you forget to bring the key to the room with you everywhere (bring it even to the kitchen or shower).

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Queens University Belfast makes the application process really easy. They send you all the documents they need and after you submit them, you receive an acceptance letter. They also accept the language documentation from KU, based on your English grade from high school.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: Queens University makes the application process really easy. They send you all the documents they need and after you submit them, you receive an acceptance letter. They also accept the language documentation from KU, based on your English grade from high school.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: the hos university was really helpful and would answer all questions within a few days.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I chose my modules by looking at the course catalogue. However, when I arrived two of my modules was changed to fully online and I therefore changed my modules when arriving. I had made sure to get a lot of modules accepted beforehand (forhåndsgodkendt), so that i could change without having to go through the process again. But one of the new modules had to be accepted while i was in Belfast, but it was not more complicated than sending a few mails to University of Copenhagen and submitting some documents.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: I would advise you to just follow the instructions from both Universities, they have made it very easy.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I had 'Gender and the Law', 'International Criminal and Transitional Justice' and 'Public International Law' and they were so interesting modules. They are taught law in a different way in this University as they focus more on the legal studies and critical thinking regarding laws. So there is not the same focus on the actual laws and articles as we are used to in Denmark. I really enjoyed all three modules but if I had to recommend one it would be Public International Law because the lecturer Dr. Yassin Brunger was such a good lecturer. She creating interesting debates and it was always important to have read to material for her classes. I loved every one of her classes. We had to hand in essays in all the modules and all three deadlines were in December.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: As mentioned, law is taught differently as they focus more on the critical thinking and the aim of the law rather than the use of the actual law and articles within it. But I enjoyed the switch and seeing law from a different angle.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: 'Gender and the Law', 'International Criminal and Transitional Justice' and 'Public International Law'.

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I would recommend all three. Gender and the law focused on feminism and the view on women and how that view is visible through laws and the legal system. International Criminal and Transitional Justice was about the large sized humanitarian crimes such as genocide and how you achieve transitional justice through different mechanisms. Public international law is the same module as International Law in University of Copenhagen, just with focus on the critical thinking rather than the different international laws.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Things are in general cheaper and with the grant from Erasmus + SU from Denmark (and some personal savings, everything should be great.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: There was a lot of trips afforded by the Queen's University Accommodation to the must-see attractions in Belfast, which are all very cheap compared to taking the trip privately. This included the Titanic Museum, a bus tour around historical areas for protestans and catholics in Belfast.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: A lot of activities at the Treehouse in BT9 too that you should attend. Its a cafe with free tea and coffee and games to play, a great place to make new friends.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: make friends with the other international students too as you all can explore the city together.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Definitely take a weekend trip to Dublin with the bus. I also booked a flight to London for a weekend (very short flight). It is a bigger city and has places to go too. In Belfast, there is so much nature and I really enjoyed Whitehead, Cavehill and Giant's causeway. I also loved the St. George's Market that is also opened in the weekends.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Very easy. It is a smaller city and people are very helpful and kind. You get to know the city really quick and it was good walking to the city, around 30 min walk to the city centre from BT9.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Do a lot of things in the beginning especially as that's the best time to make new friends. Time flies and after a while you fall into a routine with the people you know. Not the say you can't make new friends, but its definitely easier though the activities provided by the accommodation.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Not that big of a culture difference.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Very very friendly and talkative people, which was so nice.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
(1) raincoat and umbrella (rains a lot and you will walk a lot) 
(2) nice slippers or "home" shoes (for when you walk around the kitchen or to the Treehouse to wash clothes and so on 
(3) Not to worry about clothing (they are way more relaxed with clothing than in Copenhagen)

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Really interesting history in Belfast, make sure to explore it and find out more about the "Troubles". You can book a walking tour where you will be guided through historical events and areas of Belfast. Take the hop-on-hop-off bus and explore the peace wall.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Improving my English skills by attending classes, reading material and writing essays. Getting to know both the northern irish culture and all the other international cultures. Living in a small village of students and becoming friends with people from all around the world.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: I will warn you that the mattress is not that comfortable and there was a lot of issues with the shower head in the showers. Furthermore, the walls are rather thin so you can hear if people are coming back from a night out, but you kind of get used to it after a while. But the maintenance issues were definitely the biggest challenge. Everything else was great.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: I hope you choose Belfast, it is a great city with so much history! Not to big of a city so you feel at home quickly and can get around the city by walking.

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
